name: Circular Waste Systems
region: Global (Japan, China, India, West Africa, Mesoamerica, Northern Europe)
summary: Waste-as-resource loops where outputs of one process become inputs for another — composting, night soil recycling, biochar, nutrient cycling, and closed-loop craft production.

claims.statement: Edo-period Japan (1603–1868) operated a near-zero-waste urban economy: human waste was sold as fertiliser, broken ceramics were repaired with lacquer (kintsugi), and old clothing was recycled through multiple use-cycles down to paper fiber
Chinese night soil systems sustained intensive agriculture for 4000+ years without synthetic fertilisers, as documented by F.H. King's comparative study of Eastern farming
West African compound farming integrates livestock waste, crop residues, and household organics into soil fertility management, maintaining yields on the same plots for centuries

evidence.source: Hanley (1997) Everyday Things in Premodern Japan: The Hidden Legacy of Material Culture, University of California Press
King (1911) Farmers of Forty Centuries: Organic Farming in China, Korea, and Japan, Mrs. F.H. King
Fairhead & Leach (1996) Misreading the African Landscape: Society and Ecology in a Forest–Savanna Mosaic, Cambridge UP
McDonough & Braungart (2002) Cradle to Cradle: Remaking the Way We Make Things, North Point Press

notes: Resolves 2 inbound links (terra_preta, regenerative_agriculture). Edo Japan is the most complete historical example of industrial-scale circular economy. The modern 'circular economy' movement is rediscovering principles that were standard practice for millennia.
